_comment: CoE 2.0 model parameters. None of these are hardcoded in the scripts that use them -- change values here to run experiments without touching code. The 'elo' section is the only one build_elo.py reads right now; 'hybrid' and 'coe' are placeholders for later phases (build_hybrid_coefficients.py), documented here now so the full intended structure is visible from day one.

elo._comment: k, home_field, and offseason_retention were calibrated via calibrate_elo.py's grid search (K in [10,15,...,40], HFA in [0,25,...,100], retention in [0.5,0.6,...,1.0]) against the full 2000-2026 dataset (18969 games), optimizing out-of-sample Brier score. Best found at the time: K=35, HFA=50, retention=0.8 (Brier=0.18359, vs 0.18684 for the original placeholder guess). Full 210-row results in data/processed/elo_calibration_results.csv. k IS NOW 40, NOT 35, and the two numbers are not interchangeable: k only ever acts on the record through k * M, so it belongs to whichever performance multiplier is configured below. 35 was fitted against MOV, whose M averages 2.43; xSRDiff's averages 1.66, so keeping 35 across the switch would have quietly cut every rating update by a third and made the comparison a test of k rather than of the layer. 40 is xSRDiff's own optimum, chosen on 2002-2017 only (the search never saw 2018-2026) with home_field and offseason_retention held at the values above -- a joint refit of all three under the new layer is still owed. mov_c/mov_d remain the UNCALIBRATED FiveThirtyEight-NFL-derived placeholder; they are inert while modifier is 'xsrdiff' except on the handful of games that take the fallback.

hybrid._comment: elo_weight/coe_weight calibrated via calibrate_hybrid_weight.py's grid search (0.25 through 1.00 in steps, an initial coarse pass at [0.25,0.40,0.50,0.60,0.75] showed monotonic improvement all the way to the edge, so the grid was extended to find the real optimum) against the full dataset, optimizing out-of-sample Brier score (same walk-forward methodology as calibrate_elo.py). Best found: elo_weight=0.85, coe_weight=0.15 (Brier=0.18718). Notably, pure Elo (elo_weight=1.0) scored WORSE (Brier=0.18814) than this blend -- confirming the frozen 5yr CoE component adds real predictive signal on top of Elo alone, even at a small weight, which validates the hybrid architecture's core premise. Full 10-row results in data/processed/hybrid_weight_calibration_results.csv. difficulty_alpha (below) is deliberately NOT tuned this way -- see calibrate_hybrid_weight.py's docstring for why (CoE measures achievement, not prediction accuracy, per spec section 32). RE-CHECKED after the xSRDiff switch and k=40 (2026-09-26): the layer changes the Elo component these weights blend, so the fit was run again. The optimum moved to elo_weight=0.80 (Brier 0.17704) against 0.85's 0.17707 -- a difference of 0.00003, which is noise, so the weights were deliberately LEFT ALONE rather than chased. On the new ratings the blend scores 0.17707 against pure Elo's 0.17832 over the same 27,296 games, so the premise below still holds.

coe._comment: win_base/ot_loss/regulation_loss/difficulty_alpha are the Game CoE 2.0 formula constants, deliberately NOT tuned via Brier score/prediction accuracy (see calibrate_hybrid_weight.py's docstring for why -- CoE measures achievement, not prediction). tie_delta is the spec's own suggested starting formula for a tie (G_tie = 1 + tie_delta*(0.5 - p_this), symmetric around 1.0, rewarding an underdog for tying and mildly penalizing a favorite for settling for one) -- defaulted to match difficulty_alpha's value as a reasonable placeholder, not yet independently calibrated. Only matters once the dataset extends before 1996's overtime rule; ties were structurally impossible in 2000-2026.

hfa._comment: Team-specific home-field advantage (src/hfa.py, src/build_hfa.py). ANALYSIS ONLY: build_elo.py still uses the flat 'elo.home_field' above; nothing here changes production Elo. Every value is an untuned placeholder to be chosen by out-of-sample backtesting (log loss / Brier), not by intuition. half_life_years: L in the recency weight w = 2^(-age_years / L). shrinkage_k: K in lambda = N_eff / (N_eff + K). fcs_prior_weight: alpha in prior = alpha * H_FCS + (1 - alpha) * H_FBS -- currently inert because the database stores FBS-vs-FBS games only, so every prior falls back to the FBS baseline. effective_n_method: 'sum_weights' (N_eff = sum of w, the starting definition) or 'kish' ((sum w)^2 / sum w^2); pluggable in src/hfa.py. point_bounds: search interval, in Elo points, when converting an HFA estimate into an equivalent home bonus; a result at a bound is flagged rather than trusted.

performance._comment: Which performance multiplier M scales the Elo update (src/srdiff.py). 'mov' is the margin-of-victory multiplier the project used through PR #8. 'xsrdiff' is the strength-adjusted Success Rate layer (EXP-03): M = clamp(1 + beta * SR+, m_min, m_max), where SR+ is how far the WINNER's Success Rate differential beat what the venue-adjusted pregame Elo gap implied. 'raw_srdiff' (no strength adjustment) and 'result_only' (M = 1) exist for the backtest matrix. A game with no per-game Success Rate on both sides, or in a season no point-in-time expectation fold covers, takes 'fallback' and records that in elo_game_history.performance_model -- missing SR is never treated as 0. beta/m_min/m_max ARE NOW CALIBRATED, not placeholders. They were chosen on 2002-2017 alone, over beta in [8,12,16,20,24] x bounds {[0,5],[0.1,3]} x k in [20,25,...,50], and then scored on 2018-2026, which the search never saw: Brier 0.18677 against MOV's 0.18825 at MOV's own best k of 35, log loss 0.55101 against 0.55444, accuracy 0.7115 against 0.7055, calibration error 0.01567 against 0.01629. The pooled margin is small enough that a game-level bootstrap cannot separate it from zero, so the evidence this rests on is consistency: xSRDiff predicted better in 7 of the 9 held-out seasons, losing only 2023 (-0.00133) and drawing 2026, and a bootstrap that resamples whole seasons rather than games puts the mean gain at +0.00141 Brier, 95% CI [+0.00044, +0.00231]. beta=16 tied it in-sample (0.17993 vs 0.17999, a difference with no meaning) and beta=12 was taken on the tie because its multiplier spread is narrower: it sends 14% of games to the m_min floor against beta=16's 18%. The floor and the ceiling were then varied independently, because sweeping them as pairs confounds them: the ceiling is worth about 0.0004 Brier (5.0 beats 3.0) and the floor is worth 0.00006 across m_min from 0.0 to 0.25, i.e. nothing. So m_min stays at 0.25 rather than 0 -- srdiff.py's loader refuses a zero floor on purpose, and the sweep gives no reason to weaken that guard. At 0.25 a win in which the winner was outplayed still moves ratings, a quarter as far; that is this layer's real mechanism and its main risk. Re-run src/backtest_performance_layer.py after any data change; full matrix in data/processed/performance_layer_backtest.csv. Note the scale difference: MOV's M averages 2.43 and xSRDiff's 1.66, so k in the 'elo' section above belongs to this choice and must be refitted with it, never carried across.

coe2_bonuses._comment: Explicit season/postseason bonus terms for CoE 2.0 (spec's B_(i,Y)), applied by src/build_coe2_rollups.py AFTER game awards: C = sum(Game CoE 2.0) + B. Each awarded bonus is stored as its own row in team_coe2_bonuses with its category, count and reason, so no bonus can hide inside opponent strength and a season total is always decomposable. ALL VALUES SHIP AT 0.0 ON PURPOSE: the categories and the machinery are implemented and tested, but the magnitudes are a modelling decision to make with the validation harness, not defaults to inherit. At 0.0 a season total is exactly the sum of its game awards, so the current model stays reproducible. Bonuses are derived from real results only -- bowl/CFP participation from the games table, first place in the derived conference standings -- the playoff model's own ordering, which starts in 2014 and is NOT the conference championship game, national titles from data/reference/national_champions.csv -- and never from ratings. Bump 'version' when changing any value so old and new rows stay distinguishable.

simulation._comment: Bracket simulator (src/coefficients/simulate_bracket.py). temperature was fitted by calibrate_sim_temperature.py against real results: the CoE gap ENTERING each season (end_year = Y-1, so every game scored is out of sample) against the actual winner, home perspective only, on the 5,081 games since 1980 where BOTH teams were top-40 by entering CoE -- the population a 24-team bracket actually contains. Best found: T=4.5 (Brier=0.22356, calibration error=0.02034) against the previous hand-picked T=6.0 (Brier=0.22845, calibration error=0.07760): the old value was systematically underconfident, pulling every matchup toward a coin flip. The Brier curve is flat between about 4.25 and 5.0, so treat T as 'about 4.5', not a precise constant. Fitting on ALL games instead gives T=3.0, which scores worse here: a slope tuned mostly on mismatches does not transfer to a bracket. Full search in data/processed/sim_temperature_calibration.csv.
simulation._home_field_comment: home_field is the host's edge in CoE points, applied in the ROUND OF 24 ONLY, where the higher-CoE team hosts. calibrate_sim_temperature.py measured it at about 1.25 CoE points by fitting it jointly with the temperature, so it is not absorbed into the slope. It was previously recorded here as 'measured_home_field' and deliberately NOT applied, on the argument that CoE already decides who hosts and applying it would count the same advantage twice. That argument was wrong and the value is now live: CoE decides WHICH team hosts, but carries nothing about the advantage OF hosting, which is a venue effect measured on real games. Omitting it understated the host in all eight Round-of-24 games. From the Round of 16 on, nothing in draw_playoff_bracket_v2.py assigns a host, so those rounds are neutral and get no venue term -- they stay exactly symmetric. Set to 0.0 to return to the neutral-everywhere model.
